exchanges.question: No analyst question; IR asked participants to limit themselves to two questions.
exchanges.answer: Procedural only; no substantive content.

exchanges.question: How much of the ~500bp deceleration implied by the 9%-11% September guide is supply constraints versus FX, and what are the broadening supply constraints beyond advanced SoCs? Second: is Apple seeking more memory sourcing flexibility to secure supply and mitigate memory inflation, or to preserve customer value proposition?
exchanges.answer: Parekh: FX is a ~2.5 percentage point sequential headwind to YoY growth and supply constraints increase significantly sequentially, affecting iPhone, Mac and iPad; combining the two gets close to the June growth rate. Cook: June constraints were primarily on Mac, lesser on iPhone and iPad, driven by availability of advanced nodes for SoCs and high demand; very significant constraints currently with limited flexibility to remedy. Memory: paid significantly more in June than March, partially offset by carry-in inventory; September memory costs even higher, partly offset by carry-in inventory (decreasing benefit beyond September) and lower non-memory component costs; beyond September market memory pricing continues to increase and could drive an increasing impact. DRAM market has three suppliers; more suppliers could help supply, unclear on pricing; evaluating all options.

exchanges.question: Expected adoption of the Apple Upgrade leasing program across the install base and whether it shortens replacement cycles for iPhone, Mac and iPad. Second: learnings from the iOS 27 / Siri AI public beta, whether Siri AI drives holiday iPhone demand, and how usage informs compute costs and recovery through iCloud+.
exchanges.answer: Apple Upgrade makes it easier to get latest products via leasing; Apple residual values generally much higher than competitors; offered in Apple retail stores, not widely in all channels, and only in the U.S. (Parekh); uptake to be seen, early feedback quite positive. Siri AI developer and public beta feedback overwhelmingly positive. On compute cost it is early going and Cook does not want to say Apple has a complete plan; there will be upgrade possibilities on iCloud+ for heavy users. No adoption rate or replacement-cycle quantification given.

exchanges.question: How much do supply constraints hit the December quarter, given the Street models 8%-9% growth there? Second: could Apple broaden silicon suppliers (e.g., the Arizona fab) in a reasonable time frame to alleviate constraints?
exchanges.answer: Cook: primary constraint is advanced nodes for SoCs; root cause is a demand forecast issue, with iPhone (+22%, also +22% year-to-date) and Mac (+29%) doing remarkably better than expected; Apple has been pulling supply ahead and will be scrambling on supply this quarter. Parekh: these dynamics plus FX are built into the 9%-11% September guide; no color or guidance beyond the September quarter. On suppliers, Cook said it is not a partner or supplier issue; Apple sources over 100 million components this year out of Arizona as part of the $600 billion U.S. commitment and is pleased with that fab's ramp.

exchanges.question: Will Apple pursue multi-year LTAs with suppliers at pre-agreed prices, and in pricing does it aim to protect product gross profit dollars or gross margin? Follow-up: drivers of services slowing to 12% (slightly below guide) and further implied deceleration below 10% in fiscal Q4; is App Store/AI reprioritizing time a factor?
exchanges.answer: Cook: Apple reluctantly raised prices due to a '100-year flood' in memory pricing with exponential increases; it weighs units, revenue and margin over the long term, not a formula or 90-day clock; LTA question not addressed. Parekh: from 16% in fiscal Q2 to 12% in June, FX was the main driver; also the year-ago F1 theatrical release (favorable to year-ago June and September quarters), mobile gaming headwinds in App Store, App Store business model changes in certain countries, and U.S. court ruling on link-outs (Supreme Court will hear appeal). App Store still set a June quarter record; roughly met expectations but a bit more softness in mobile gaming. FX is ~5 percentage point headwind to services YoY growth from March to September quarter, another ~2.5 point sequential headwind June to September.

exchanges.question: Has there been pull-forward of demand ahead of memory-driven price increases (consumer, enterprise, education), and is it factored into the outlook? Second: does AI at the edge open additional addressable markets for Apple?
exchanges.answer: iPhone has run at 22% growth year to date; pull-forward is not obvious in the data. Apple has now raised prices on iPad and Mac; too early to conclude on price elasticity given channel inventory and consumer response lag; will understand more in the weeks ahead. Enormous AI opportunities; running some percentage of requests on device is strategic and a competitive weapon; no specific new markets named.

exchanges.question: Will Siri AI change Apple's capital intensity given back-end requests to first-party and third-party cloud? Second (to John Ternus): is the competitive landscape changing with OpenAI's potential AI device or a SpaceX AI phone?
exchanges.answer: Cook: hybrid model of third-party cloud and own data centers; Apple has been growing OpEx and spending quite a bit more on AI, with AI costs also in COGS; Siri AI cost impact to be seen, offset by iCloud plan upgrades, balance uncertain. Ternus: reiterated there is much opportunity in the space; Apple focused on its plans; no comment on specific competitors.

exchanges.question: Update on Siri AI rollout in China and Europe and hurdles to launch there. Follow-up: sequential gross margin walk from ~48% ex-tariff refund in June to ~46.5% guide midpoint ex-refund; FX versus commodity costs?
exchanges.answer: Cook: working closely with the European Commission; not yet able to launch Siri AI in the EU on iPhone/iPad, but it is or will be offered on Mac there since Mac is not covered by the same regulations; in China, received approval last week to ship original Apple Intelligence features (e.g., cleanup), more work required for Siri AI. Parekh: GM fell 120bp from 49.3% (March) to 48.1% ex-tariff refund (June), more than 100% explained by memory cost; the 160bp step from 48.1% to the 46.5% midpoint ex-refund is likewise more than explained by memory; partial offsets from carry-in inventory, lower non-memory component costs and favorable mix; FX minimal.

summary.overview: JPMorgan Chase earned $16.9B, or $6.14 per share, in Q2 2026 with a 23% ROTCE, as equities markets revenue rose 86% and IB fees 30%. Jeremy Barnum, CFO, raised NII ex-Markets guidance to ~$96.5B from $95B and adjusted expense guidance to ~$107.5B, while Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO, said conditions are "getting close to as good as it gets."
keyTakeaways: Barnum said the first-half capital markets complex beat expectations by $6.5B, driving $1.5B of booked expense plus an implicit $1B for the second half.
Barnum said this quarter's equities drivers (major IPOs, index rebalancing, Korean market dynamics) are statistically improbable to repeat.
Dimon elevated two co-presidents and said his succession timetable is unchanged at "several years" or "a few years," up to the board.
Barnum put excess capital at ~$40B to deploy over time, and Dimon set a 17% return goal on deployed capital, open to adjacency M&A but organic first.
financialHighlights: Net income was $16.9B and EPS $6.14 including significant items, with expenses of $27.3B (+15% YoY).
CIB revenue rose 27% to $24.9B on net income of $9.7B, with IB fees up 30%, equities up 86% and fixed income up 6%.
CCB revenue rose 8% to $20.3B with net income of $5.3B and over 500,000 net new checking accounts.
Credit costs were $2.5B, including $2.4B of NCOs and a $149M reserve build, and CET1 fell 20bp to 14.1%.
guidance: Jeremy Barnum, CFO, raised FY2026 NII ex-Markets to ~$96.5B from $95B, with total NII ~$105.5B and Markets NII ~$9B.
Barnum raised adjusted expense guidance by $2.5B to ~$107.5B, and Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO, said expense growth might slow in 2027 or 2028.
Barnum guided the card net charge-off rate to ~3.2% and kept consumer deposit growth at low single digits.
Barnum declared a $1.65 quarterly dividend effective 3Q and expects IB activity to remain healthy on a "quite robust" pipeline.

qa.question: What drove the NII ex-Markets raise, and why is Markets NII guided higher despite higher rates?
qa.answer: Barnum cited deposit balances and mix as the main driver of the $95B to $96.5B raise, implying a higher exit rate, and said lower non-interest-bearing financed assets lift Markets NII, with ~$150M shifting there from a higher CIB equity allocation.

qa.question: Isn't operating leverage positive with 15% revenue growth, and why is Troy right to run the consumer bank?
qa.answer: Barnum broke down the $2.5B expense raise into $1.5B already booked from $6.5B of capital markets outperformance and $1B added for the second half, not a revenue view; Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO, agreed leverage was positive and cited Troy's analytics and operations expertise.

qa.answer: Dimon cited almost 1,000 AI use cases, about 50 important, with some areas cutting jobs 30% or 40%, but said benefits accrue to customers; Jeremy Barnum, CFO, named IPOs, index rebalancing, Korean equities and Asia activity.

qa.question: How healthy is the consumer, and why buy back stock at three times tangible book?
qa.answer: Barnum said consumer spend is solid across income segments with delinquencies a little lower than expected, and JPM buys less as price rises against ~$40B of excess capital; Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO, said he "made a mistake" citing $20B before.
qa.read: Answered partially; no buyback amount given.

exchanges.question: What do the management changes (Doug and Troy elevated to co-presidents, Marianne's departure) mean for leadership development and Dimon's CEO tenure? Second: how sustainable are IB and markets strength, and how risk-on is the firm?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: board made two co-presidents to prepare them to do more; timetable unchanged; Marianne chose to retire rather than stay once she knew the plans; 'No mystery.' Barnum: IB fees were fine but not super peak by historical standards; there was some pull forward and large deals contributed meaningfully, but the pipeline is quite robust and activity seems to beget activity; declined to guide. Equities' particular events this quarter hard to imagine repeating; markets revenues elevated with more financial resource deployment. The market is extremely risk on and JPM is a taker of that, balancing client support with caution.

exchanges.question: Progress toward the 15% retail deposit market share goal and how higher-for-longer rates affect the pace of share gains. Follow-up: where is JPM in the investment cycle (branches, AI, bankers) and what does it mean for medium-term operating leverage?
exchanges.answer: Wholesale deposit growth strong in first half, outperforming expectations, helped by lending (BFI, data centers) creating deposits. Consumer deposit growth expectation of low single digits this year unchanged; strong net new checking offset by yield-seeking flows, which remain a risk given a more hawkish rate environment. No change to the 15% aspiration, seen as a long-term outcome of strategy. On expenses, Dimon said it is a complete continuation with no change expected; Barnum said JPM will always invest while delivering exceptional current returns; no operating leverage outlook given.

exchanges.question: Drivers and 3Q/4Q cadence of the upward NII ex-Markets revision and exit rate into next year. Follow-up: why is markets NII guided higher despite higher rates?
exchanges.answer: NII ex-Markets raised from $95 billion to $96.5 billion; implied second half suggests a higher exit run rate assuming forwards and current deposit expectations. Biggest driver is deposit balances across wholesale and consumer plus favorable mix; rates slightly higher at both ends; actual rate sensitivity likely above reported EAR due to consumer beta outperformance, mostly front end. Markets NII is liability sensitive but forecast up due to expected lower non-interest-bearing financed assets in the second half; also higher equity allocation to CIB moves roughly $150 million of NII from NII ex-Markets to markets NII, which would not be offset in NIR.

exchanges.question: What characteristics are Dimon and the board seeking in the next CEO? Is Dimon's remaining tenure fixed or rolling, with a longer stay as executive chair, given Marianne's departure read as an extension? Follow-up: what does 'no change in timing' mean?
exchanges.answer: Timing essentially the same and up to the board. Listed traits: management, people, analytical, detail, culture carrier, curiosity, heart, grit, soul, work ethic, ability to work with CEOs and prime ministers; 300,000 employees, 50,000 in branches, 150,000 in operating and call centers. Named two co-presidents, Jen Piepszak as COO and Mary Erdoes continuing to run AWM. Timetable is 'several years', 'a few years', plus or minus, totally up to the board.

exchanges.question: With negative adjusted operating leverage year to date, could expense growth slow and operating leverage emerge over the next few years given AI? Second: any update on regulatory proposals (G-SIB surcharge, Basel III)?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: margins went up this quarter; perpetual operating leverage is a 'crazy notion' and part of why banks failed 20 years ago; might see a slowdown in expense growth in 2027 or 2028; will spend where ROI is good; AI benefits ultimately accrue to customers. Regulation: four changes needed—remove double count in operational risk capital, remove double count in market risk capital ($80 billion+ of market risk capital vs biggest quarterly loss of $1.4 billion; CCAR market loss ~$14-15 billion), adjust G-SIB as intended since 2015, fix short-term wholesale funding; would hold 10% more if asked but not with falsely done numbers. Barnum: removing RWA from the STWF denominator disproportionately burdens banks with both markets and consumer businesses (JPM, Bank of America) versus former investment bank competitors.

exchanges.question: Is this as good as it gets, or is it earlier cycle given AI, defense spending and supply chains? Second: is there a rate tipping point where deposit volumes and betas change meaningfully?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: getting close to as good as it gets; don't know how long it lasts. Barnum: short answer is they don't really know; expected negative convexity in consumer rate paid by now but not experiencing it; at some point it kicks in. Stress tests model accelerating rate paid in a regime change; current EAR ignoring convexity could wrongly suggest a 7% rate environment is great, which would not hold if they had to reprice the deposit franchise. Dimon: they assume some of that in models.

exchanges.question: Isn't operating leverage positive in dollars with 15% revenue growth, and why is this 'as good as it gets'? Second: what gives confidence Troy, without consumer experience, is right to run the consumer bank?
exchanges.answer: Dimon agreed operating leverage was positive. Barnum: expense guidance revised up $2.5 billion; first-half capital markets complex outperformed expectations by $6.5 billion with $1.5 billion of associated additional expense already booked; implicitly added $1 billion for the second half, not to be read as a revenue view. Dimon: very healthy, exuberant market with high prices and volumes, unknown duration. On Troy: strong analytics, EQ, culture carrier, operations/technology expertise from the IB; cross-company experience important. Barnum corrected that Troy was an options trader, not an FX trader.

exchanges.question: Are AI efficiency benefits underestimated, and could banks restructure much leaner (as Block did cutting 40% of staff)? Follow-up: what was most exceptional in equities this quarter that may be hard to sustain?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: not a sensitive topic; expects huge efficiency in certain parts; almost 1,000 use cases, about 50 really important (risk, fraud, marketing, hedging, prospecting, note-taking, idea generation, document reading); discrete areas reduced jobs 30% or 40% with most offered jobs elsewhere; retraining; AI will be faster and dramatic but benefits accrue to customers, not a sustained 50% ROE; big topic at July offsite. Barnum: equities drivers were major IPOs, major index rebalancing, complicated Korean equity market dynamics, Asia activity and very active clients; statistically improbable to repeat that combination.

exchanges.question: What is the health of the Main Street consumer amid housing/rate fragility, and is CapEx broadening beyond AI? Follow-up: why buy back stock at three times tangible book rather than hold more excess capital, and what about M&A?
exchanges.answer: Some CapEx and loan growth appears non-AI but AI proliferates widely. Dimon: CapEx ~$4 trillion a year; AI CapEx went from $400 billion last year to $700 billion this year, projected a little over $1 trillion next year. Consumer: spend robust across income segments, tax refund tailwind, delinquencies a little lower than expected, little support for K-shape; negative real wage cohort a watch area; credit depends on labor market, surprisingly resilient. Capital: buy less as price rises; excess capital approximately $40 billion expected to deploy over time; won't tell the market what they'll do. Dimon: 'made a mistake' mentioning $20 billion, could do far more or nothing; goal is deploying capital at a 17% return; open to inorganic (adjacencies, data) but organic first; building Chase UK toward a European digital bank.

exchanges.question: Status, timing and target audience of the smart cash tool, and comments on paying more for money over time? Second: what are JPM's European consumer banking aspirations in aggregate?
exchanges.answer: Smart cash is still a test case relating to a narrow segment of accounts competing for investment and deposit business; tests coming out; 'You'll see something this year.' Europe: digital changed the calculus; Chase UK started 4 or 5 years ago with almost 3 million or 2.5 million UK customers; opened in Berlin, doing better in Germany than expected but not yet profitable; added investment products in the UK, likely to add elsewhere and probably credit card. Dream is a pan-European successful digital bank; patient.

exchanges.question: Are competitors' credit underwriting standards getting looser? Second: could regulatory stability arrive and enhance bank valuations?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: 'crazy' is a strong word; data center underwriting is a bellwether; JPM passed on some deals (power supply, tenant risk) under a precise framework; competitive but normal pressures; flexes for important clients but tries to hold the line. Dimon: described a very mild deterioration—revenue growth assumptions, expense add-backs, more PIK, weaker covenants, rollover risk—in some players; expects outliers in the next credit cycle. Barnum: regulatory stability desirable and getting closer; not convinced regulation is a major valuation drag for JPM. Dimon: Supreme Court decision on presidential removal power reduces flip-flopping; praised Bowman and Warsh reviewing rules; resolution and recovery does not work; discount window should be viewed differently.

exchanges.question: Beyond volume/revenue-related expense, is JPM raising other expense categories or pulling forward tech/marketing? Second: how nimble is CIB capital allocation, is it at peak, and are internal limits binding?
exchanges.answer: Some ups and downs including marketing strategy he would not disclose; main driver is volume and revenue-related expense. Token (AI model) expense trivial in the first half, forecast meaningful acceleration in the second half but full-year still trivial and partly budgeted; important for next year; use the right model for the right purpose including open source. Declined to discuss internal limits; capital allocation responds to client demand plus passive effects (volatility raising market risk capital, equity appreciation raising prime RWA); ample excess capital; system flush with capital but less with liquidity, liquidity regulation next on the agenda. Dimon: risk standards unchanged.

summary.overview: Eli Lilly grew Q2 2026 revenue 48%, with MOUNJARO and ZEPBOUND at $14.9B and non-GAAP EPS of $8.38 after $3.03 of acquired IPR&D charges. Lucas Montarce, CFO, raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $85B-$87B, and the call centred on the Foundayo launch, the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge and retatrutide's BLA pathway.
keyTakeaways: Ilya Yuffa, President of Lilly USA, said Foundayo volume nearly doubled versus a month earlier, about one in four new starts is on it, and prescribers rose to 36,000 from 8,000.
Yuffa said the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, launched July 1, expands obesity coverage by about 35%, with an estimated 60%-70% of its patients new to therapy.
Dave Ricks, Chair and CEO, said retatrutide is expected to be submitted as a BLA by Q1 2027, pending more CMC data and active litigation over its classification.
Montarce said U.S. ZEPBOUND net price will fall as CVS access from Q4 reduces medical exceptions, which is embedded in guidance.
financialHighlights: Revenue rose 48%, with U.S. revenue up 33% on volume and U.S. price down 3%, or 9% excluding favorable rebate estimate changes.
Gross margin rose about 1.3 points to 86.3%, and the non-GAAP performance margin rose 9 points to 54.8%.
Marketing, selling and administrative expenses rose 25% and R&D rose 14%.
Constant-currency revenue grew 55% in Europe (including a $250M Jardiance milestone), 30% in Japan and 93% in China.
guidance: Lucas Montarce, CFO, raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $85B-$87B and the non-GAAP performance margin to 49%-50.5%.
Montarce set non-GAAP EPS guidance at $35.50-$36.50, a $2.78 midpoint increase before absorbing $3.03 of Q2 IPR&D charges.
Montarce said H2 growth slows because favorable rebate adjustments should not recur and 2025 included a MOUNJARO new-country launch bolus.
Dave Ricks, Chair and CEO, expects Foundayo's U.S. Type 2 diabetes regulatory action later this year, with major international launches at the start of 2027.

exchanges.question: How does Lilly see the consumer/self-pay obesity market evolving (including aesthetic-driven approaches), and how similar is the U.S. self-pay market to the international one?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Obesity treatment utilization is still mid-single-digit in the U.S. and globally; access is improving with Bridge and some state Medicaid programs going live or committing to next year, obesity TRxs are around 3 million, and about 55% of ZEPBOUND prescriptions are self-pay; Lilly is investing in consumer awareness and expanding LillyDirect. Jonsson: outside the U.S. obesity is still mainly out of pocket; Lilly is replicating U.S. consumer practices and has launched versions of LillyDirect OUS, but models will differ because regulations differ.

exchanges.question: Why has the U.S. Foundayo launch curve been slower than anticipated and when will it inflect; and how are OUS competitive dynamics shaping up as Novo scales its oral pill, including Novo's claim of 50% UAE share within three weeks?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Focus is on physician education, access/affordability and consumer awareness; CVS added Foundayo in June, Bridge launched July 1 and full DTC began; in the last week of July volume was almost doubling versus a month ago and around one in four new starts is on Foundayo, which Yuffa called an inflection point. Jonsson: UAE launched early May with a strong start, most patients incretin-naive, and Lilly's combined incretin share held steady despite a second oral; Mexico and Saudi launch next, most launches in 2027, with no supply gating; early data is noisy and often sell-in reflecting inventory build.

exchanges.question: What are the requirements and milestones for retatrutide to be accepted as a BLA, and would that classification be unique to retatrutide or extend to subsequent incretins?
exchanges.answer: Lilly believes retatrutide is a biologic under the amino acid count rule and as analogous to a protein; the first court decision was mixed and litigation is active, and Lilly hopes to reach a conclusion with FDA supporting a BLA. All clinical data needed to submit is in hand but more CMC data must be gathered; Lilly is in communication with the agency and will update investors on filing status. Submission expected by Q1 next year; Ricks cited a large lead over any triple-acting competitor.

exchanges.question: What are the early learnings and ramp from the Medicare obesity (GLP-1 Bridge) rollout, and how are orals versus injectables tracking?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Bridge increases obesity-therapy access by about 35% more Americans; it is early but showing a significant inflection, with prior authorization working and criteria clear, and LillyDirect enabled to fulfill Bridge. ZEPBOUND and MOUNJARO both inflected over the last few weeks, partly from Bridge; around 80% of patients are on injectables, and an estimated 60%-70% are new patients who had no access before.

exchanges.question: Does retatrutide need a commercial strategy against unauthorized versions available today or will approval solve it; and does its higher efficacy open indications beyond tirzepatide's?
exchanges.answer: People are awaiting authentic retatrutide and are expected to 'vote with their feet' once it is approved. Higher efficacy opens new opportunities: knee osteoarthritis pain reduced by 75% in TRIUMPH-4 and TRIUMPH-1; a MASH/MASLD study is ongoing where glucagon action may be unique; a chronic lower back pain study reads out sometime next year; several further indications are being evaluated internally.

exchanges.question: What is the post-Verzenio breast cancer strategy given the oral SERD and oral PI3K, and is an all-oral combination planned?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly Oncology and Head of Business Development
exchanges.answer: The key breast cancer targets are ER, CDK4/6 and PI3K alpha; Lilly believes it has the best medicine for each and plans to combine them all. EMBER-4 adjuvant trial for imlunestrant (INLURIYO) reads out next year; the tersolisib (PI3K inhibitor) phase III is about to begin, initially with existing endocrine therapies plus investigator's-choice CDK4/6 (largely Verzenio), later combining with INLURIYO, enabling an all-oral combination.

exchanges.question: Guidance seems to imply H2 revenue deceleration versus Q2 despite Bridge and Foundayo access; is something on price being missed or is it conservatism?
exchanges.answer: The full-year guide was raised by $2.5 billion; prior-period adjustments to U.S. rebate and discount estimates (including this quarter) are not expected to continue in H2. The H2 2025 base included the bolus of MOUNJARO launches in new countries, which will not recur, so percentage growth slows though dollar growth stays significant and future OUS growth comes from penetration. Europe Q3 seasonality and U.S. Type 2 diabetes Q4 seasonality are factored into the guide.

exchanges.question: Which regions are driving OUS MOUNJARO growth, and what is happening in India with generic semaglutide launches and reported capacity constraints?
exchanges.answer: MOUNJARO holds market leadership across many markets; China NRDL achieved category leadership after 16 months, with significant growth in Korea, the U.K., Mexico and Germany, and share in many markets similar to or above the U.S. In India and Brazil MOUNJARO TRx kept growing after generic semaglutide launched, attributed to superiority data; in Canada tirzepatide TRx grew at the same pace as the total market; generic makers are seeing significant supply constraints.

exchanges.question: How extensive is Foundayo sampling and is it dampening IQVIA prescription data; and can Lilly quantify expansion of the U.S. prescriber base?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Sampling covers the first 30 days of the first dose, typical for a retail oral small molecule, extensive across prescribers and fully supplied. Prescribers rose to 36,000 from 8,000 cited on the last earnings call, with week-on-week progress; the effect of sampling on IQVIA data was not addressed directly.

exchanges.question: ZEPBOUND net price is about $580 per prescription, above cash price; how sustainable are medical exceptions now CVS is back on formulary, and are they behind the recurring favorable rebate adjustments?
exchanges.answer: Pricing is transparent: LillyDirect $299 to $449 and Bridge $245, plus commercial; script size also drives the per-prescription figure, so price per pack is significantly lower. CVS access starting in Q4 will reduce medical exceptions, which are a short-term thing; Lilly expects price to go down, which is embedded in guidance, and to more than offset it with volume growth.

exchanges.question: Are psychiatry and vaccines areas Lilly can scale as a priority, or are the deals one-offs driven by the science?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly Oncology and Head of Business Development
exchanges.answer: Both areas share immense unmet need, the through line of internal and BD work; assets were bought at prices that keep Lilly disciplined and create long-term value, similar to other deals year to date. He declined to forward look on building further in infectious disease or psychiatry, saying Lilly will be opportunistic based on what is available.

exchanges.question: Which one or two non-obesity pipeline assets should the Street pay more attention to?
exchanges.answer: Cardiovascular: PCSK9 gene editing plus oral and injectable Lp(a)-lowering drugs; neuroscience: psychiatry, sleep-wake via Centessa, and addiction and major depressive disorder possibly via incretin science; oncology is probably the richest readout period in Lilly's history, highlighting Kelonia's in vivo CAR T for multiple myeloma and AJ1-11095 JAK inhibitor. Immunology: growth of the drug transcribed as 'empagliflozin' with new indications, plus combinations in IBD and psoriatic diseases; he called it the strongest pipeline Lilly has ever had even excluding incretins.

exchanges.question: Given Foundayo UAE sales of $31 million versus $67 million in the U.S. (analyst figures), what is the ex-U.S. obesity potential; and will ex-U.S. governments reimburse Foundayo for diabetes better than tirzepatide given a lower price?
exchanges.answer: Encouraged by UAE but it is very early, data is noisy and includes initial inventory build; most patients are incretin-naive, showing need for an oral in obesity and Type 2 diabetes. Major OUS rollout happens at the beginning of 2027. Lilly is probably slightly better positioned for Type 2 reimbursement with an oral and three head-to-head trials, but OUS reimbursement always takes time, so launch focus will be chronic weight management.

summary.overview: Chipotle grew Q2 2026 revenue 9.3% to $3.3B on a 2.2% comp, including a 1% transaction gain, while restaurant-level margin fell 220bp to 25.2% and adjusted EPS was flat at $0.33. Adam Rymer, CFO, raised the full-year comp guide to low single digits but guided Q3 to about +1%, assuming a ~200bp Cyclospora-related softening that began in late July continues.
keyTakeaways: Rymer said comps softened about 200bp in the second half of July amid the industry Cyclospora issue, which Scott Boatwright, CEO, said hits sales though Chipotle is not involved.
Rymer expects pricing and inflation to match from Q4 after a first half with pricing near 1% against low-to-mid 3% inflation.
Boatwright said younger and lower-income cohorts improved most and Q2 delivered the highest YoY wallet share gains since 2024.
Digital sales reached $1.3B, or 38.3% of sales, up from 35.5%, which Boatwright tied to the rewards relaunch and Summer of Extras.
financialHighlights: Revenue rose 9.3% to $3.3B, with comps of +2.2% on about 1.6% menu price and +1% transactions.
Restaurant-level margin fell 220bp to 25.2%, with cost of sales up about 80bp to 29.7% on beef, freight and higher usage.
Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.33, flat YoY, and non-GAAP G&A was $176M.
Chipotle repurchased $631M of stock at an average $32.55, added $1.3B of authorization and ended with $800M of cash and no debt.
guidance: Adam Rymer, CFO, raised FY2026 comp guidance to low single digits and guided Q3 to about +1%, or roughly 3% underlying before the Cyclospora headwind.
Rymer expects Q3 menu price in the mid 2% range, with the full year near the high end of 1%-2%.
Rymer guided Q3 cost of sales just under 30%, labor in the mid 25% range, other operating costs mid 15% and non-GAAP G&A around $180M.
Scott Boatwright, CEO, expects about 350 openings in 2026, HEAP in about 2,000 restaurants by year-end and a national catering launch in 2027.

qa.question: What underlies the low-single-digit comp guide, including Q3 to date?
qa.answer: Rymer said traffic improved into early July before a ~200bp softening in late July tied to the Cyclospora issue, and Q3, the toughest lap, is expected at about +1% if that impact continues.

qa.question: Does the ~1% Q3 guide imply ~3% underlying, and where is Max 15 throughput?
qa.answer: Rymer confirmed it, said the duration is very difficult to predict, and put Max 15 at low 20s in-store, mid-teens digital and low-to-mid 30s combined, with HEAP stores two or three entrees higher.

qa.question: What is the margin outlook beyond Q3 as the price-inflation gap narrows?
qa.answer: Rymer said Q3 inflation should be about 3% against mid-2% pricing, and from Q4 the two should match.

qa.question: Why is 350 company openings a year right versus the prior 400 ceiling?
qa.answer: Boatwright said going beyond 350 risks diminishing returns, and extra growth will come from Western Europe and partners, noting Alshaya has 15 restaurants with acceleration in 2027.

exchanges.question: Do repeat 'pantry' LTOs like Chicken al Pastor still deliver equal or better lift each time they return; and is value perception improving to reflect generous portions and long-standing underpricing versus the industry?
exchanges.answer: Chipotle Honey Chicken performed better the second time, as many LTOs do, though there is likely a point of diminishing returns around the fifth or sixth time; menu innovation has ramped to 4x what it was a couple of years ago with new items coming in the months ahead. The brand tracker showed solid value-perception progress across all income groups and age cohorts, and Q2 affordability scores were the best in probably the past couple of years; value also includes convenience, execution, innovation and the high-protein menu.

exchanges.question: Investors push back that Chipotle is spending a lot to get only 1%-2% same-store sales growth; what gives confidence that momentum builds into 2027 despite tough comparisons and recent slowdown?
exchanges.answer: Q2 transaction growth reflected early Recipe for Growth results, especially menu innovation, while HEAP, throughput and hospitality investments show proof points in guest satisfaction, food quality and consistency. Additional drivers — menu innovation, deeper rewards engagement, stronger brand communication and group occasions — are showing green shoots and will build through H2 2026 into 2027; he cited unshared digital ideas from Arlie Sisson and creative ambition from Fernando Machado.

exchanges.question: What underlies the full-year low-single-digit comp guide, including Q3 to date, the recent softening and expected cadence?
exchanges.answer: Traffic improved through Q2 and into the first half of July; in the second half of July comps softened about 200 basis points amid the industry Cyclospora issue. Q3, the toughest lap of the year, is expected at around plus 1%, assuming that roughly 200 basis point impact continues; year-to-date performance and Q3/Q4 plans supported raising the full-year guide to low single digits. Boatwright: Chipotle is impacted on sales but not involved in the Cyclospora issue; implicated products are not on its menu and its lettuces are sourced in California.

exchanges.question: What is the incremental capex, expected sales uplift and timeline of refreshing 1,000-1,500 North American stores; and would Chipotle use partners in other international markets instead of owning stores?
exchanges.answer: Chipotle has never done an aesthetic remodel; it is stage-gating a remodel/refresh program this year across several locations and geographies at $100,000-$300,000 per restaurant to test returns, with nothing to report yet. Internationally it will own and operate Western Europe and grow from that base, with the rest of the world partner-operated via partners such as Alshaya (Middle East), Alsea (Latin America) and SPC (Southeast Asia), through partner-operated or JV structures.

exchanges.question: Digital sales grew about 18% year over year after accelerating four quarters ago; was there a big catalyst, and is it linked to changes at the register around loyalty and payment?
exchanges.answer: It is all linked: last year's Summer of Extras taught what works in digital, informing the rewards relaunch that removed app friction and added flexibility to earn and redeem, and this year's Summer of Extras accelerated digital revenue. Chipotle also benefited from an emerging trend, and Arlie Sisson's holistic approach should bring 'game changing' digital commerce innovation over the coming weeks and months.

exchanges.question: Will HEAP labor savings all be reinvested into the production line, and could that drive traffic and customer satisfaction?
exchanges.answer: Yes; HEAP yields about two to four hours of efficiency depending on volume, which is kept in-restaurant for morning prep and peak line deployment, lifting Max 15 throughput, total sales and taste-of-food scores. HEAP will be in 2,000 restaurants by year-end, with the entire portfolio hoped to be complete sometime in 2027; all new restaurants come standard with HEAP.

exchanges.question: Why is 350 company-operated openings per year the right level versus the prior ceiling of 400, and what is the gating factor to accelerating above 350?
exchanges.answer: Given U.S. white space and the ability to develop ready-now leaders, one restaurant per day is meaningful growth the organization can support; going beyond 350 risks diminishing returns in openings or fracturing the base. Incremental growth will come from company-owned Western Europe and partner-operated markets, which will ramp quickly — Alshaya already has 15 restaurants across three or four countries after a couple of years, with meaningful acceleration for 2027 — so Chipotle can still target its historical growth number.

exchanges.question: With a new brand chief, where will positioning go given the For Real campaign may have gone stale, and will value and ingredient quality be highlighted more prominently versus limited-service competitors?
exchanges.answer: For Real was extraordinary and served the brand for many years; Fernando Machado's work is the next evolution, not a 180 pivot. Expect more on fresh in-restaurant prep, ingredient usage and cultivating a better world, with stretched creative ambition; value will be highlighted not via price points or discounts but as the best ingredients prepared fresh daily, with abundance and speed at an approachable price point.

exchanges.question: Does the roughly 1% Q3 comp guide imply about 3% underlying trend with a 2% Cyclospora headwind assumed for the rest of the quarter; and where is system Max 15 throughput for non-HEAP stores?
exchanges.answer: Yes, that is correct; expense guidance is based on the 1% comp guide assuming the impact continues through the quarter, which is very difficult to predict. HEAP restaurants do about two or three more entrees in Max 15; overall in-store is in the low 20s, digital (almost 40% of sales) in the mid-teens, and combined low to mid-30s per restaurant per day.

exchanges.question: What is working in promoting loyalty in-restaurant and what can improve; and do the roughly 80% of in-store transactions without loyalty over-index to lower-income guests?
exchanges.answer: No, non-loyalty in-store transactions are broad-based rather than lower-income. The current experience of fumbling with the app and a card is 'clunky'; in August Curt's team will introduce one-stop pay that earns points on payment and allows enrollment, running behind the scenes without burdening crews or throughput. More consumer education on loyalty in-restaurant is needed.

exchanges.question: Are the new menu items coming in the months ahead center-of-the-plate items or sides, and what detail can be provided?
exchanges.answer: The culinary team has been expanded to drive new news, not just pantry items; work is focused on center-of-the-plate items, with teams also on beverages, sides and desserts. Some big ideas have been pushed through the stage-gate process and could appear on the calendar maybe in the back half of 2026, but certainly in 2027.

exchanges.question: How did Q2 and Q3-to-date trends look by age and income, and are pressured younger and lower-to-middle income cohorts improving relative to higher income, including frequency differences?
exchanges.answer: The younger and lower-income cohorts improved the most; Q1 into Q2 results were broad-based but with outsized impact in those groups, driven by Chipotle Honey Chicken, Cilantro Lime Sauce, promotions like the Matchday BOGO and rewards. Boatwright: Q2 saw the highest year-over-year wallet share gains since 2024, and Chipotle has taken share in each month of 2026 across all income and age cohorts.

exchanges.question: What is the margin outlook beyond Q3, including the gap between pricing and inflation narrowing near year-end?
exchanges.answer: The price-inflation gap was widest in the first half, with pricing in the 1% range versus inflation in the low to mid 3%. In Q3 inflation is expected closer to about 3% with pricing in the mid 2% range, and from Q4 forward the two are expected to match, eliminating the dislocation.

exchanges.question: Did the World Cup create regional divergences that benefited Chipotle; and what has the methodical pricing rollout taught, giving comfort to trend toward the high end of the 1%-2% guide?
exchanges.answer: About 300 restaurants within roughly 10 miles of World Cup stadiums saw a 50 to 100 basis point comp benefit during the tournament, but the overall quarter impact was less than five basis points. The rolling market-by-market pricing approach is working, allowing precise measurement of resistance and adjustment to inflation; Chipotle will continue the strategy, and the dislocation was just a timing impact.

exchanges.question: How much do LTOs contribute to frequency and traffic given the stepped-up cadence; and do high-protein offerings attract existing guests or a new cohort?
exchanges.answer: No specific LTO lifts are disclosed, but Chipotle Honey Chicken and Chicken al Pastor raised transactions from frequent guests and new guests, typically hundreds of basis points of transaction lift mostly sustained through the promotion, with stickiness after; seen as a multi-year AUV lever. Boatwright: protein LTOs bring in new customers, and trying an LTO materially raises lifetime value; expect a couple more center-of-the-plate items in H2 plus sides and a more meaningful push into beverage.

summary.overview: Kinsale grew Q2 2026 diluted operating EPS 15.9% to $5.54 with a 75.5% combined ratio and 24.4% annualized operating ROE, even as gross written premium fell 5% on shrinkage in the Commercial Property Division. Excluding that division GWP rose 3.7%, and the company added a $250M buyback authorization while its pricing trend fell 5.9%.
keyTakeaways: Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, called commercial property "definitely a buyer's market" and said Kinsale is writing a shrinking volume there.
Stuart Winston, Chief Underwriting Officer, said London competition is spreading into long-tail casualty lines and depressing Construction pricing.
Kehoe raised buyback capacity to $337M and called it the principal capital allocation strategy while growth is limited.
Salmaan Allibhai, Chief Analytics and Technology Officer, put casualty loss cost trend at probably mid-single digits with little social inflation.
financialHighlights: Diluted operating EPS was $5.54, up 15.9% from $4.78, with net income up 31.1% and net operating earnings up 13.3%.
Gross written premium fell 5% and net written premium 1.4%, while net earned premium rose 8.9%.
The 75.5% combined ratio included 4.5 points of favorable prior-year development and 1.3 points of cat losses.
The expense ratio rose to 21.7% from 20.7% on a higher net commission ratio from larger reinsurance retentions.
guidance: Bryan Petrucelli, CFO, said the Q2 expense ratio of 21.7% is a good measure going forward, with a possible slight commission uptick after the June 1 reinsurance renewal.
Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, said Commercial Property comparisons ease modestly in H2 because 60% of the division's premium was written in last year's first half.
Stuart Winston, Chief Underwriting Officer, said nine new products launched this year, five more launch imminently and 10 are in the pipeline.
Petrucelli cited new money yields around 5.25% and average duration of four and a quarter years.

qa.question: When will property pricing reach equilibrium, should the accident year loss ratio drift up with mix, and how will buybacks be paced?
qa.answer: Kehoe had no insight on timing and said Kinsale will keep leaning into buybacks with about $80M left on the prior $250M plus a new $250M; Salmaan Allibhai, Chief Analytics and Technology Officer, said the loss ratio could drift up over time.
qa.read: Answered partially; no timing or loss ratio figure.

qa.question: Is inbound account growth from broker engagement or pricing, and what are casualty loss trends?
qa.answer: Winston said both, with an idle broker initiative re-engaging lapsed brokers and steady hit ratios; Salmaan Allibhai, Chief Analytics and Technology Officer, put casualty loss trend at mid-single digits, and Michael Kehoe said IBNR release is being slowed in longer-tail lines.

qa.question: What drove the better current accident year loss ratio, and will the ceding commission keep rising?
qa.answer: Allibhai cited normal variability with losses below expectations and reserves as conservative as ever; Bryan Petrucelli, CFO, said only one month of the June 1 treaty is in Q2, so a slight commission uptick may be offset by AI efficiency.
qa.read: Answered partially; no loss ratio driver isolated.

qa.question: How much are casualty ROEs compressing as E&S softens?
qa.answer: Kehoe said everything is managed to a 20% ROE or greater, most lines run ahead of it, and quarterly ROE was 24.4%.
qa.read: Answered partially; broker commission question not addressed.

exchanges.question: What drove the improvement in the current accident year loss ratio vs 2Q25, unlike other commercial insurers (non-cat property, mix, loss picks)? Follow-up: will the ceding commission rate on reinsurance keep rising after the renewals?
exchanges.answer: Allibhai: losses came in below expectations as in the last few quarters; nothing out of the ordinary, normal variability and mix across a dozen statutory lines; reserves are as conservative as ever in company history. On commissions: acknowledged normal tension between wholesalers, retailers and buyers, worse in a soft market; argued Kinsale offers the best service (quote ratio, response time) and broadest risk appetite, and continues to grow ex the Commercial Property Division, which is going through a unique correction. exchanges.question: Is 2Q the trough for commercial property, with larger players pulling out; could pricing become less negative in 2027 or could Kinsale return to large shared placements? Follow-up: what is driving the 3.7% growth ex large account property, is business returning to the admitted market, and what would make growth inflect?
exchanges.answer: No telling where property goes in 2027; still pressure from London MGAs and traditional markets on shared and layered deals, larger limits, stretch primaries; Kinsale will price to return thresholds and accept shrinking in that division. London competition is creeping into other long-tail liability occurrence lines, depressing Construction pricing, with more competition in general casualty; Kinsale will lean into pockets of opportunity. There is some flow to the admitted market but it is not pervasive.

exchanges.question: How much of the increase in inbound accounts cited in the press release comes from broker engagement vs more competitive pricing? Follow-ups: view on social inflation and casualty loss trends; and was the accident year loss ratio benefit entirely short-tail property?
exchanges.answer: Winston: a bit of both; the idle broker initiative is re-engaging lapsed brokers; hit ratios roughly the same for renewal and new business, so submission growth means more binds. Kehoe: language added to explain confidence in the model; Commercial Property crisis is over and rates are coming down dramatically, but the underlying business model works. Allibhai: casualty loss cost trend probably mid-single digits, varying by line; little social inflation seen given smaller accounts and lower limits; short-tail lines performing especially well, across the board. Kehoe: being more conservative, slowing IBNR release in longer-tail occurrence business and letting it flow faster in short-tail lines.

exchanges.question: Granularity on property pricing in Q2 vs Q1 and when it might reach equilibrium? Follow-ups: with mix shifting from more-profitable property to casualty, should the current accident year loss ratio drift up; and how will buyback pacing evolve?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe: equilibrium will come eventually since cats do happen, but no insight into when; other property divisions see growth. Winston: Agribusiness Property and small business property are more stable; Inland Marine (five product buckets) seeing a little more competition; people are starting to get to the floor of property pricing, still pressure from London. Allibhai: hard to say, loss ratio could drift up over time; losses below expectations; Kehoe: IBNR conservatism is a positive indicator. Buyback: will continue to lean in; first $100 million authorization exhausted, then $250 million with about $80 million left, plus the new $250 million; principal capital allocation strategy while growth is limited, growth remains first priority when it accelerates.

exchanges.question: How has product expansion contributed to growth over the past year, and what is the potential growth uplift from new products going forward?
exchanges.answer: New products are rolled out at a crawl, walk, run pace, never jumping in feet first. They are creating growth, driving submissions and new premium, but it will be slow growth; will ramp up as the market turns. No quantification given.

summary.overview: Deere grew fiscal Q3 2026 net sales and revenues 5% to $12.608B and earned $1.379B, or $5.10 per share, as construction and forestry sales rose 18% and production and precision ag fell 6%. Deere raised FY2026 net income guidance to $4.75B-$5B, and Deanna Kovar, President of Worldwide Agriculture & Turf, called 2026 the ag cycle bottom with a measured 2027 recovery.
keyTakeaways: North American planter and sprayer early order programs are up mid-single digits versus last year's completed program, with See & Spray factory adoption nearly doubling.
Brent Norwood, CFO, said net tariffs will be a 2027 headwind, with the run rate near $1B versus about $750M net this year.
Chris Seibert, Director of Investor Relations, said C&F orders cover four to five months versus a typical two to three, on infrastructure, data centers and rental fleets.
Deere lowered its South America ag industry outlook to down 15%-20% and Europe to about flat.
financialHighlights: Equipment operations net sales rose 6% to $10.999B with a 14.4% operating margin, including $110M of tariff refunds.
Production and precision ag sales fell 6% to $3.998B, with operating margin of 13.2%.
Small ag and turf sales rose 12% to $3.383B with an 18.4% operating margin.
Construction and forestry sales rose 18% to $3.618B on 8 points of price, with a 12.1% operating margin.

guidance: Dan Pooley, Manager of Investor Communications, raised FY2026 net income to $4.75B-$5B and equipment operations cash flow to $5B-$5.5B.
Pooley guided PPA sales down about 10% (11%-12% margin), small ag and turf up about 15% (14.5%-15.5%) and C&F up about 20% (10.5%-11.5%).
Chris Seibert, Director of Investor Relations, cut FY2026 direct tariff expense to about $1.1B from $1.2B, assuming no further refunds.
Brent Norwood, CFO, expects Q4 PPA and C&F sales similar to Q3, with lower PPA and small ag margins on seasonal costs and no refund benefit.

qa.question: Is the net 2026 tariff impact a headwind, tailwind or neutral for 2027?
qa.answer: Norwood said about $1.1B of direct tariffs less $382M of refunds leaves roughly $750M net this year, and next year's run rate is closer to $1B, a step up.

qa.question: What lowered the tariff estimate to $1.1B, and how is the excavator launch going?
qa.answer: Seibert said Section 232 import rates fell from about 25% to 15% from June 1, covering five of 12 months and implying a 2027 tailwind; Brent Norwood, CFO, said three Deere-designed excavator models are shipping.

qa.question: Why does C&F price fall in Q4 after +8% in Q3, and how big could dealer rental become?
qa.answer: Seibert said Q3 lapped about 5% negative price a year earlier and full-year C&F price is 3 points; Brent Norwood, CFO, said 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as rentals but gave no size target.

qa.question: How does 2027 production versus retail set up, and what pricing should be expected?
qa.answer: Seibert said PPA and C&F are each underproducing retail by a couple of points this year; Deanna Kovar, President of Worldwide Agriculture & Turf, said pricing aims to cover inflation without a figure.

exchanges.analyst: None (scripted management discussion led by Dan Pooley)
exchanges.question: Not an analyst exchange: scripted results review and moderated management discussion (Q3 performance, guidance changes by segment, model year 2027 early order programs, dealer inventories, precision ag technology, closing thoughts) before analyst Q&A opened.
exchanges.answer: Q3 results and FY2026 outlook given (see metrics and guidance); Q3 included $110 million of incremental IEPA tariff refunds, FY2026 refunds $382 million, no further refunds assumed; direct tariff expense ~$1.1 billion for FY excluding refunds. C&F backlogs extend well into fiscal 2027, producing modestly below retail; PPA order books effectively full, South America industry revised to down 15%-20%, underproducing retail there. North American EOP orders for planters and sprayers up mid-single digits vs completion of last year's program; management views 2026 as the bottom of the ag equipment cycle with a measured, not sharp, recovery in 2027. Used MY2023-2024 high-horsepower tractor inventory down nearly 40% YoY; See & Spray factory adoption to nearly double (about 1/3 of NA sprayers on order); over 40% of MY2027 NA planters with advanced offerings.

exchanges.question: Setup for 2027: production vs retail by region; and with EOP up mid-single digits, what are 2027 pricing expectations given concerns about farm equipment cost inflation?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: modest underproduction this year in PPA and C&F, a couple percentage points for each; PPA driven by caution in South America, C&F by retail growth with orders four to five months out. Kovar: EOP pricing rolled out several months ago; focus remains on covering inflation with pricing across EOP products and the PPA portfolio for 2027. No specific price figure given.

exchanges.question: What drove the tariff expectation falling to $1.1 billion (tariff relief for ag equipment in July or refunds)? Follow-up: update on the excavator launch and timing of broader adoption.
exchanges.answer: Seibert: FY2026 run rate updated from $1.2 billion to $1.1 billion, excluding refunds, mainly from Section 232 changes (roughly 25% rate on imported goods dropped to 15%, given European imports); effective 1st June, so five of 12 months this year, implying a further tailwind in fiscal 2027. Norwood: first Deere-designed excavator models launched this spring, three models in market, shipments getting to customers, very positive feedback; more models roll out over the next three to four years; early days.

exchanges.question: Did shipments slip from 4Q into 3Q, and does the inventory-to-sales ratio suggest Deere built tractor inventory in 3Q ahead of the industry; how is the cadence exiting the year?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: don't read too much into Q3; shipment plans set for the year with orders on hand; pulled ahead some demand to manage Q4 risk; nothing to be concerned about on inventory. Kovar: sold-ahead positions and retail pace on trend with historical averages; North America tractor shipments started slowly and are catching up. Norwood: PPA and C&F Q4 net sales similar to Q3; no refund benefit in Q4; PPA and SAT margins lower in Q4 on seasonal high R&D and SA&G.

exchanges.question: How might mix, especially higher technology sales in C&F and precision ag EOP take rates, influence 2027, relative to the 2- to 3-point mix benefit discussed in stronger years?
exchanges.answer: Too early to tell; uncertainty from input and commodity volatility, shipment disruptions (Black Sea), recent softness in the E.U. and Brazil; construction fundamentals good and its growth could affect mix; EOP tech adoption and how the programs and combines wrap up will drive mix. Encouraged by signals but no figure given.

exchanges.question: What regional variability is there in the EOP, and could the mid-single-digit growth end in the high single-digit range as the programs wind down?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division, PPA, Sales and Marketing, Americas and Australia
exchanges.answer: A couple of weeks remain on sprayer EOP and a bit longer on planters; U.S. trending slightly better than Canada, which is a very limited part of the planter business; time will tell whether mid-single digit turns more positive. Best signals are technology take rates: doubling of See & Spray on factory-installed sprayer orders and 40% of planters taking the most advanced planting technologies.

exchanges.question: Has the cadence of EOP orders been driven by recent grain price improvement or by technology decisions; were orders already up a month and a half ago?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division, PPA, Sales and Marketing, Americas and Australia
exchanges.answer: Wouldn't read much into cadence, which has been as expected; EOP tweaked this year to give dealers more choice; pleasantly surprised by technology take rates; hopeful the mid-single digit increase holds.

exchanges.question: Are 8 Series tractor orders tracking the better EOP trend in North America? And will Europe, with heat and input cost stress, respond to a crop price recovery the way the U.S. would?
exchanges.answer: 8R orders as expected; orders four to five months out; model year 2026 shipment schedule basically closed, collecting Q1 orders; corn futures about $5.05 a good signal. Brazil runs a three-month order book; Q4 orders in hand, industry guide changed, too early to tell for 2027; the move financing program at single-digit rates may help. Europe mixed: arable farmers more challenged, Small Ag & Turf supported by stable dairy and livestock cash flows; overall order pace as expected, no recent step-up.

exchanges.question: How are C&F order programs shaping up, and how much is dealer rental fleet loading and what is the outlook for that theme?
exchanges.answer: C&F order trends very positive: about four to five months of orders on hand vs typical two to three months. Drivers: large infrastructure projects, data center starts, independent rental channel participation and dealer-owned rental fleet opportunity; 2026 underproduction gives a 2027 opportunity. No quantification of rental fleet loading.

exchanges.question: Given remaining Section 232 benefit in 2027 and no further refunds in Q4, is the roughly $800 million net 2026 tariff impact a headwind, tailwind or neutral for 2027, all else equal?
exchanges.answer: Net tariffs will be a headwind into next year: about $1.1 billion direct tariffs less $382 million refunds gives net exposure of approximately $750-ish this year; next year run rate expected closer to right around $1 billion, a step up in tariff expense versus this year.

exchanges.question: C&F pricing: why does guidance imply lower price in Q4 versus +8% in Q3? And how large could Deere's dealer rental business become and how does it change the economics?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: C&F price guide started the year at 2.5%, moved to 3%, rounded down to 2.5%, now back up (full-year 3 points); Q3 +8% partly an easy comp against about 5% negative price in Q3 2025 from incentives; Q4 orders in hand, nothing outsized, road building contributes. Norwood: opportunity to increase rental exposure via independent rental houses and dealers; 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as a rental and growing; dealer appetite to expand rental fleets could boost inventory fill next year; no size target or economics given.

exchanges.question: What merchandising incentives and EOP pricing trends imply for margins next year (up, down, neutral)? And what does the FTC right-to-repair settlement mean for the aftermarket business and the $2 billion-$3 billion lifecycle parts opportunity over five years?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: taking measured inflationary price, committed to cover inflation over time, nothing outsized; pricing set at several points in the year; inflation dynamic (oil prices, supplier tariffs). No margin direction given. Norwood: Deere has always supported customers' ability to repair their own equipment, unchanged; agreement formalizes existing tools such as John Deere Operations Center PRO Service (diagnostics, digital manuals, self or independent software updates); supports long-term lifecycle solutions aspirations. No comment on the $2 billion-$3 billion figure.

exchanges.question: Will the 2028 European CAP budget policy change pull demand forward into 2027 or cause farmers to delay; any directional 2027 forecast for Europe?
exchanges.answer: Too early to tell; order book four to five months out, just collecting Q1 orders; arable sentiment depends on input costs and commodity prices, dairy and livestock fairly stable. Too early to say whether policy pulls demand forward or delays it; no 2027 forecast.

exchanges.question: How are Brazilian and U.S. farmers positioning on input costs and how might that affect crop and equipment decisions?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division, PPA, Sales and Marketing, Americas and Australia
exchanges.answer: Uncertainty on input prices everywhere; fertilizer impact differs between Brazilian and U.S. farmers; farmers looking for alternatives in products, amounts and sources. Not seeing a huge reduction in intended application; still focused on yield; larger farmers have multiple years of inputs contracted and are reconsidering.

summary.overview: Apple's June quarter revenue rose 16% to a record $109.4B, with iPhone up 22% to $54.3B and Mac up 29% to $10.4B despite supply constraints; diluted EPS rose 29% to $2.02 including $0.11 of tariff refunds. Kevan Parekh, CFO, guided September revenue growth to 9%-11%, down from the 14%-17% June guide, on a roughly 2.5-point FX headwind and supply constraints expected to increase significantly. Tim Cook, CEO, said this was his final earnings call.
keyTakeaways: Tim Cook, CEO, blamed the advanced-node SoC constraint on demand running ahead of forecast, not suppliers, with constraints broadening from Mac to iPhone, Mac and iPad in September.
Cook said Apple reluctantly raised iPad and Mac prices amid a "100-year flood" in memory pricing, with costs higher again in September.
Services growth slowed from 16% to 12%, which Kevan Parekh, CFO, attributed mainly to FX plus the F1 compare, mobile gaming softness and the U.S. link-out ruling.
Siri AI arrives this fall; Cook said Apple has no complete plan yet for recovering compute costs beyond iCloud+ upgrade tiers, and cannot yet launch it on iPhone and iPad in the EU.
financialHighlights: Revenue $109.4B (+16%) with June quarter records in every geographic segment; products $78.7B (+18%), services $30.7B (+12%).
iPhone $54.3B (+22%), Mac $10.4B (+29%), iPad $6.2B (-6% on the A16 iPad compare), Wearables $7.9B (+6%).
Gross margin 50.1% including about 2 points of tariff refunds; 48.1% excluding them versus 49.3% in March, a decline Parekh said memory costs more than explain.
Net income $29.8B, EPS $2.02 and operating cash flow $34.4B were June quarter records even excluding refunds; OpEx $19.1B (+23%); $33B returned to shareholders.
guidance: Kevan Parekh, CFO, expects September revenue growth of 9%-11% (June guide 14%-17%), with FX a roughly 2.5-point sequential headwind and constraints across iPhone, Mac and iPad.
Parekh expects mid-teens iPhone growth and services growth similar to June's 12% after a further 2.5-point FX headwind.
Parekh guided gross margin to 47%-48% including about 1 point of tariff refunds (46.5% ex-refund versus 48.1%), the decline more than explained by memory.
Parekh guided OpEx to $19.1B-$19.4B, OI&E around $350M and tax around 16.5%; no color beyond September.
risksMentioned: Supply constraints on advanced-node SoCs, which Tim Cook, CEO, called "very significant" with limited flexibility to remedy.
Memory costs rising again in September and, per Cook, continuing to increase beyond it as the carry-in inventory offset shrinks.
FX: about 2.5 points sequential on total growth and about 5 points cumulative on services from March to September, per Kevan Parekh, CFO.
App Store headwinds from mobile gaming, business model changes and the U.S. link-out ruling; unknown price elasticity; Siri AI regulatory delays in the EU and China.

qa.question: How much of the roughly 500 bps September deceleration is supply versus FX, and why are constraints broadening?
qa.answer: FX is a roughly 2.5-point sequential headwind and supply constraints increase significantly across iPhone, Mac and iPad, together bridging to June's growth. Tim Cook, CEO: memory costs rose significantly from March to June, will be higher in September, and the carry-in offset shrinks after that.

qa.question: How much do supply constraints hit the December quarter, and could Apple broaden its silicon suppliers?
qa.answer: The root cause is a demand forecast miss, with iPhone up 22% and Mac up 29%, and September will be "scrambling on the supply side"; Parekh gave no guidance beyond September. Cook: "this isn't a partner or supplier issue"; Apple sources over 100M Arizona components this year.
qa.read: Declined to quantify December; pushed back on supplier premise.

qa.question: Will Apple pursue multi-year supplier LTAs, protect gross profit dollars or margins, and why did services decelerate?
qa.answer: Pricing weighs units, revenue and margin over the long term, not a 90-day clock; LTAs went unaddressed. Parekh: services fell from 16% to 12% mainly on FX, plus the F1 compare, mobile gaming and the link-out ruling.

qa.question: Where does Siri AI stand in China and Europe, and how much of the gross margin decline is FX versus commodities?
qa.answer: Apple is working with the EU commission and offers Siri AI on Mac there; China approved original Apple Intelligence features last week. Parekh: the 120 bps drop to 48.1% and the 160 bps drop to 46.5% are each more than explained by memory, with FX "a pretty minimal impact".

unanswered.question: How much do supply constraints hit the December quarter?

exchanges.question: How much of the roughly 500 basis point deceleration implied by the 9%-11% September revenue guide is supply constraint versus other factors like FX, and what are the supply constraints that are broadening beyond the advanced SoCs discussed last quarter? Follow-up: are Apple's reported efforts to seek greater memory sourcing flexibility about securing supply and mitigating memory inflation, or about preserving the customer value proposition?
exchanges.answer: Kevan: September total company revenue is expected to grow 9%-11% year-over-year, impacted by two factors: FX is a sequential headwind of about two and a half percentage points to the year-over-year growth rate from June to September, and the impact from supply constraints is expected to increase significantly sequentially, affecting iPhone, Mac and iPad; combining those two gets pretty close to the June total company growth rate. Tim: June constraints were primarily on Mac and to a lesser extent iPhone and iPad, driven by very high demand and the availability of the advanced nodes the SoCs are produced on, with less flexibility in the supply chain than normal; constraints are currently very significant with limited flexibility to remedy them. On memory: Apple paid more in the March quarter than December, significantly more in June than March (partially offset by carry-in inventory), and expects to pay even higher memory costs in September, partly offset by carry-in inventory (a benefit expected to decrease beyond September) and lower costs on certain non-memory components; beyond September, market memory pricing continues to increase, which could drive an increasing impact on the business. The DRAM market has primarily three suppliers; more suppliers would help on the supply side and perhaps pricing (unclear); Apple is evaluating all options.

exchanges.question: What adoption rates does Apple expect for the Apple Upgrade program across the two and a half billion device install base, and will it shorten the iPhone replacement cycle or equally benefit Mac and iPad, which have not had U.S. device subsidies? Follow-up: what are the learnings from the iOS 27 and Apple Intelligence public beta, will Siri AI be an iPhone demand driver this holiday, and how does beta usage inform compute costs and recovery of those costs through iCloud+?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Apple Upgrade makes it easier for customers to get the latest products with a leasing plan; residual values on Apple products are generally much higher than competitors, so it is a fairly affordable way in for customers who upgrade on a schedule; it is offered in Apple retail stores and not widely in all channels, uptake remains to be seen but early feedback is quite positive. Kevan: it is only available in the U.S. right now. On Siri AI: the developer beta was released immediately after the WWDC keynote and the public beta a few weeks ago, with overwhelmingly positive feedback from developers and reviewers; Tim called private, personal-context, OS-integrated AI a very big idea. On compute cost it is early going and Apple does not have a complete plan; it expects some people to use it a lot and will have upgrade possibilities on iCloud+ so users can buy up the stack. No adoption rate, replacement cycle or holiday demand figures were given.

exchanges.question: The Street had 12% September growth and the 9%-11% guide could be explained by FX alone; with the Street at 8%-9% for December, how much do the supply constraints hit the December quarter? Follow-up: could Apple broaden its silicon providers (e.g. the other company building a fab in Arizona) in a reasonable time frame to alleviate the constraints?
exchanges.answer: Tim: the primary supply constraint is the advanced nodes the SoCs run on; the root cause is a demand forecast issue rather than a regular supply issue, with iPhone up 22% (and 22% year-to-date) and Mac up 29% doing remarkably better than Apple's already high expectations; the supply chain has less flexibility than normal, Apple has been pulling supply ahead and there is a limit, so the September quarter will be one of scrambling on the supply side. Kevan: those dynamics plus the sequential FX impact are what is built into the 9%-11% September guidance; Apple is not providing any color or guidance beyond the September quarter, including December. On broadening silicon suppliers, Tim stressed it is not a partner or supplier issue but an incredibly strong iPhone and Mac product cycle with demand beyond expectation; Apple sources over 100 million components this year out of Arizona as part of its $600 billion U.S. commitment and could not be more pleased with how that fab has ramped.

exchanges.question: On the unprecedented price increases: does Apple intend to pursue multi-year LTAs with suppliers to lock in supply at pre-agreed prices, and in pricing is the intention to protect product gross profit dollars or product gross margins? Follow-up: 12% services growth was a bit below guidance and the fiscal Q4 guide implies below 10% reported growth; what factors drive the deceleration, and is App Store softness a function of AI reprioritizing time away from the App Store?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Apple reluctantly raised prices because it is in a 100-year flood on memory pricing with exponential increases; its philosophy looks at units, revenue and margin together and makes a business judgment over the long term rather than a 90-day clock, not a mathematical formula on one dimension; the multi-year LTA question was not addressed. Kevan: services growth went from 16% in fiscal Q2 to 12% in June, with FX the main driver sequentially, plus the year-ago theatrical release of F1 (which benefited the June and September quarters a year ago), App Store headwinds in mobile gaming, App Store business model changes in certain countries, and the U.S. court ruling on link-out transactions (the Supreme Court will hear Apple's appeal); the App Store still set a June quarter record, cloud services, video, payment services and advertising grew strong double digits, and Apple roughly met its expectations for the quarter with a bit more softness in mobile gaming. For September, FX is a theme hitting services more than the total company: about a 5 percentage point headwind to the year-over-year services growth rate from the March to the September quarter, with another two and a half point sequential headwind versus the 12% reported in June.

exchanges.question: Given the memory pricing dynamic, has Apple seen any pull-forward of demand from consumers, enterprise or education, and is that factored into its forward views? Follow-up: as AI proliferates to the edge, does Apple see additional addressable markets evolving from AI over time?
exchanges.answer: Tim: iPhone has been running at a 22% growth rate for the last while and 22% year-to-date this cycle, and pull-forward is not obvious in the data. Apple has now had to increase prices on iPad and Mac, and it is too early to reach a definitive conclusion on price elasticity because channel inventory takes a while to adjust and consumers take a while to respond; Apple will understand more in the weeks ahead. On AI, there are enormous opportunities for Apple, he is excited about Siri AI, and the ability to run some percentage of requests on device is very strategic and a competitive weapon; no specific new addressable markets were named.

exchanges.question: Will Siri AI change Apple's capital intensity, given that some requests go to the back end in both first-party and third-party cloud despite on-device and distributed compute? Follow-up to John Ternus: how is the competitive landscape changing, including potential AI-enabled devices from OpenAI or a SpaceX AI phone bypassing carriers, and where does Apple stand?
exchanges.answer: Tim: Apple uses a hybrid model with some third-party cloud and its own data centers, and there will be a mix; OpEx has been growing with quite a bit more spending on AI, and AI expenditures also sit in other P&L lines such as COGS; Apple will see what Siri AI does on the cost side, heavy users can move up on an iCloud plan, and the balance of those is a bit uncertain at the moment. John Ternus: reiterated there is so much opportunity in everything happening in the space; Apple is really focused on its own plans and very excited; no comment on specific competitors.

exchanges.question: What is the updated status of launching Siri AI in China and Europe, which were excluded from the initial rollout announced at WWDC, and what hurdles remain? Follow-up: gross margin was 48% ex tariff refund in June and the guide is about 46.5% ex refund; how much of the sequential decline is FX versus increased commodity costs?
exchanges.answer: Tim: in the EU Apple is working closely with the commission; its desire is to launch everything everywhere at the same time but it has not been able to in the EU, Siri AI is or will be offered for Mac there because Mac is not covered by the same regulations as iPhone and iPad, and Apple hopes to reach some solution. In China, last week Apple received approval to ship the original Apple Intelligence features such as cleanup, is working through that rollout, and more work is required down the road for Siri AI. Kevan: total company gross margin went from 49.3% in the March quarter to 48.1% in June adjusted for the tariff refund, a 120 basis point change of which more than 100% is explained by the memory cost change, with FX a factor but not the main driver and partial offsets from carry-in inventory, lower non-memory component costs and favorable mix; the move from 48.1% to the 46.5% September midpoint ex refund, a 160 basis point change, is also more than explained by memory cost with the same partial offsets, and FX is a pretty minimal impact versus memory.
